steps.title: Making Port
steps.body: Port grapes are crushed, traditionally by foot in stone tanks, lagares, now often by machine or robotic pistons. After two or three days of fermentation, at about 6 to 9% alcohol, aguardente, grape spirit at about 77%, is added, stopping fermentation. The result: about 19 to 22% alcohol and 90 to 110 g/l of sugar. Wine ages in Vila Nova de Gaia or the Douro.

steps.title: Ruby and tawny
steps.body: Ruby styles age briefly in large vats, keeping dark colour and fresh fruit: Ruby, Reserve, Late Bottled Vintage, LBV, a single year bottled after 4 to 6 years in wood, and Vintage. Tawny styles age in small casks, pipes, where oxygen gives nutty, caramel notes: Tawny, Reserve Tawny, aged tawnies with 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 years, and Colheita, a single-vintage tawny.
steps.highlight: Vats for ruby; casks for tawny

steps.prompt: Match each Port to its ageing.
steps.explanation: How Port ages defines its style.

steps.title: Vintage Port
steps.body: Vintage Port is made only in exceptional years, declared by each house, about three times a decade. It's bottled after two to three years and ages for decades in bottle, throwing a sediment. Single quinta Vintages come from one estate in good, undeclared years. White and rosé Ports add lighter styles.
steps.highlight: Declared about three times a decade

steps.explanation: Aged tawny is cask-aged, a tawny style.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Port is fortified with aguardente mid-fermentation
Ruby styles age in vats or bottle; tawnies in casks
Vintage Port is declared in exceptional years
